request: How is a QALY calculated? Part 4: Over time, to a cost per QALY

spec.title: Over time, to a cost per QALY

card.title: Over time, to a cost per QALY

commands.speak: Now that each year has a weight, we can add up our running example over time.
Standard care: four years at 0.5, one bar per year, for 2.0 QALYs.
The new treatment: five years at 0.7, for 3.5 QALYs.
But a healthy year far in the future usually counts for less than one today, so future QALYs are discounted.
Each year is divided by (1 + r) to the power of how far away it is; NICE in England uses r = 3.5% for both costs and QALYs.
Watch the bars shrink: year one stays whole, and year five keeps 87% of its weight.
Summed, standard care falls to 1.90 QALYs, and the new treatment to 3.27.
The gain ΔQ shrinks from 1.5 to 1.37 QALYs.
The extra cost, ΔC = 30,000, is paid up front here, so it is not discounted.
The ICER is ΔC ÷ ΔQ: 30,000 ÷ 1.37, about 21,900 per QALY, up from 20,000.
A payer with a threshold λ of 30,000 per QALY would still say yes.
So a cost per QALY is a chain: ticks on a form, the public's trade-offs, weights times years, and a discount rate.
Every link is a choice someone made, and changing any one of them moves the ICER.

quiz.question: If the new treatment's extra benefit came 20 years from now instead of within five, what would discounting do to its ICER?
quiz.right: It raises it more: QALYs twenty years away are divided by a much bigger (1 + r) to the power t, so ΔQ shrinks while the cost paid now does not.
quiz.wrong: A later year is divided by a bigger (1 + r) to the power t.
